text: Mars: A Light That Answers

A damaged landing strands a small expedition. Recovery becomes a rescue, then a return journey carrying people and evidence. This is an engineering story with recovered qualified systems, not real survival instructions.

Water

Distress recording

Service shelter

Sediment core
A band of larger grains lies between two finer layers in this core. Their order is preserved, but their dates are not known.
Supported core
The layered core is held in its cradle for inspection.
Illuminated microscope
An intact field microscope with its own lighting, ready to examine prepared samples.
Grain images
The middle band contains larger grains; finer grains lie above and below. This core preserves their order, not their dates. The pictures do not yet tell us what moved the grains.
Calibrated spectrometer
The spectrometer has been checked against its supplied reference target.
Retained sediment
A portion of the sediment is kept in its labelled container.
Mineral spectrum
The sample produces broad, overlapping features in the scan. They do not identify one mineral clearly, so the result remains inconclusive.
Sample mass
A recorded mass measurement for this specimen.
Fine–coarse–fine; spectrum inconclusive
The core has a band of larger grains between two finer layers. Its mineral scan is inconclusive. The observations do not yet establish its age or what moved the grains.
Basin field record

The record connects the retained sediment with its larger-grained middle band and inconclusive mineral scan. Its age and how the grains arrived remain unknown; nearby outcrops may help test whether water carried them.

Divinity-light · Who Is Still Outside?

A small text workshop for curious students: discover a changed question, a repeated gesture, two voices in one scene, and a headline that a source will not support. Four connected desks, not a curriculum checklist. Catholic perspectives are named; interpretations and historical claims remain distinct. Independent experiment, not school-approved material or a test of personal belief.
Jewish law expert: love your neighbour; Jesus agrees
The lawyer answers with love of God and neighbor. Jesus tells him that he has answered correctly. Both speakers are Jewish; this is a discussion within Jewish scriptural teaching.
Law expert to Jesus: Who is my neighbour?
The lawyer asks Jesus, “Who is my neighbor?” Jesus responds with a teaching story, a parable, about a traveler on the road. Watch what Jesus asks at the other end of the story.
A priest and a Levite pass by
In the story, an injured traveler is left beside the road. A priest sees him and passes by on the other side. A Levite also sees him and passes by. The story does not tell us their motives.
Our Luke 10:33–35 paraphrase: a Samaritan tends the traveller and pays

A Samaritan sees the traveler and is moved with compassion. He tends his wounds, takes him to an inn, and pays for care. He also promises to cover further costs. Jesus makes this person the helper in his story.
Jews and Samaritans: related communities, disputed worship
Jews and Samaritans shared connections to Israel's Scriptures but disagreed about matters including the proper place of worship. Jesus is Jewish, and the helper in his story is a Samaritan.
Jesus: Which person acted as a neighbour?
Jesus asks which of the three seemed to be a neighbor to the injured man. The lawyer answers that it was the one who showed mercy. Jesus replies, “Go and do likewise.”
Leviticus: love the stranger as yourself

Leviticus says of the stranger living among the people: “you shall love him as yourself; for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt.” This instruction is in Jewish Scripture, long before the Gospel story.
The priest and Levite pass; the Samaritan stops
The story contrasts passing by with stopping to give practical care. Its helper is a Samaritan. That is a contrast between these characters’ actions, not a ranking of their communities.
The help crosses a community boundary
The traveler receives care from someone across a familiar religious boundary. The Samaritan’s help does not require the story to erase the communities’ real differences.
The question turns from “who counts?” to “who acted?”
The opening asks which people count as neighbours. Jesus's closing question asks which character acted as a neighbour. The focus changes from classifying people to examining their actions.
Neighborliness is shown in what the helper does
The final question directs attention to mercy in action. In this story, being a neighbor is not merely having the right group label.
Care for the stranger is already in Jewish Scripture
The Gospel’s discussion of neighbor-love does not start from a Judaism without mercy. The Leviticus passage already connects love of the stranger with Israel’s memory of being foreigners.
Mercy crosses the boundary from within a Jewish conversation

The Samaritan helps across a religious boundary, while Jewish Scripture already teaches care for strangers. These points do not require portraying Judaism as lacking mercy or as a failed version of Christianity.
Pharisees and scribes complain: Jesus welcomes sinners to meals

Luke introduces these stories with a complaint: “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them.” The people complaining are Pharisees and scribes in this scene. They are not a stand-in for every Jewish person.
Younger son plans to ask for a servant’s job
The younger son has spent his inheritance. He plans to return, admit his wrong, and ask his father: “Make me as one of your hired servants.” He imagines returning in a worker’s place.
Father runs to meet the returning younger son

“But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.” The greeting comes before the son’s spoken confession. The father later calls for a celebration.
Father goes out to plead with the angry older son
The older son hears about the feast, becomes angry, and refuses to enter. “Therefore his father came out and begged him.” The father does not stay inside waiting for him to become less angry.
Older son: years of service, but no feast for me

The older son says, “these many years I have served you,” and complains that he was never given even a young goat for a celebration. He calls the returning son “this your son” rather than his brother.
Father to older son: all I have is yours; he is your brother

The father replies that the older son is always with him and that all he has is his. He says they should celebrate because “this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.” The story ends here, without telling us whether the older son enters.
The father goes out to both sons
The father runs toward the returning son and goes outside to the angry son. His care is directed toward both, not only the son who came home.
The welcome is not a negotiated job offer

The younger son imagines returning as a hired servant, but the father welcomes him before such an arrangement is made. The order of the scene matters without making the son's change of heart irrelevant.
The son counts service; the father names a relationship

The older son complains that his years of service have not earned a celebration. The father answers that he still belongs and that the returning son is his brother. The complaint is heard, not simply ignored.
The older brother echoes the complaint before the story
The older brother objects to welcoming his brother home, while the earlier complainants object to Jesus welcoming people they call sinners. Both passages ask who should be welcomed.
The welcome reaches toward the critics too

The father goes out to invite the angry older brother as well as welcoming the returning son. Read alongside the opening complaint about Jesus's meals, this may invite the critics to join the welcome.
The feast is explained as reunion, not a wage calculation
The father celebrates someone lost being found. Neither the younger son's proposed job nor the older son's years of service explain the feast as a payment of wages.
The last invitation is still unanswered
The father invites the older brother to the reunion, but Luke does not say whether he enters. The ending leaves his response open rather than reporting that everyone reconciled.
The expected insider may be the one still outside

The Samaritan helps across a religious boundary, while the older brother stays outside his own family's feast. Being an expected insider does not necessarily mean acting as a neighbour or joining the welcome.
Mark: compassion leads to teaching; feeding follows
Mark says that Jesus sees the crowd and is moved with compassion because they are “like sheep without a shepherd.” He begins to teach them. The feeding follows this scene.
Mark: five loaves, two fish, everyone filled, twelve baskets

Mark reports that Jesus blesses and breaks five loaves and two fish, the disciples distribute them, and everyone eats and is filled. Twelve baskets of pieces remain; the account names five thousand men. It presents an extraordinary feeding, not simply an ordinary shared lunch.
John: Passover is near; barley loaves feed the crowd

John places the feeding near Passover. A boy has five barley loaves and two fish. Jesus gives thanks; the people eat as much as they want, and twelve baskets remain. They call it a sign and want to make Jesus king, but he withdraws.
Passover recalls Israel’s liberation from slavery in Egypt

Passover is a Jewish festival remembering the Exodus: Israel’s liberation from slavery in Egypt. John’s mention of the festival gives his feeding account a particular scriptural setting. Passover is still a living Jewish observance, not only a Christian symbol.
Exodus: bread from heaven in the wilderness
In Exodus, the Israelites receive manna as food in the wilderness. The crowd in John's later story brings up this earlier account of bread from heaven.
John: “Our fathers ate the manna” ... “I am the bread of life”

After the feeding, John records a discussion of manna. Jesus says it was not Moses who gave the bread from heaven, but his Father, and then says, “I am the bread of life.” John’s account develops a claim about who Jesus is.
Compassion moves toward a person or a crowd

The Samaritan's compassion leads to practical care for a traveller. In Mark, Jesus's compassion leads to teaching and feeding the crowd. Both stories connect compassion with a response to people's needs.
Mark moves from compassion to teaching and feeding
Mark’s narrative places the extraordinary feeding after compassion and teaching. Keeping that sequence visible makes the meal part of his portrayal of Jesus caring for the crowd.
John places the feeding beside the memory of the Exodus
John places the feeding near Passover, connecting it with Israel's memory of liberation from slavery in Egypt.
John makes the earlier bread story a question about Jesus

The crowd recalls the manna given in the wilderness. Jesus responds about his Father's gift and calls himself the bread of life. John's dialogue connects the earlier account of food with Jesus' claim about who he is.
John develops the meal through Passover and bread from heaven
The festival setting and the later manna discussion connect the meal to Israel’s Scriptures. John develops an account of Jesus’ identity through those connections.
The same feeding receives distinct emphases

Both Gospels report an extraordinary feeding. Mark places it after compassion and teaching, using the image of a shepherd. John connects it with Passover and the discussion of bread from heaven, developing his account of who Jesus is.
Luther, 1517: helping the poor is better than buying an indulgence

In 1517, Luther says that giving to a poor person or lending to someone in need is better than buying an indulgence. An indulgence concerned penalties associated with sin, not permission to commit a new sin. His statement gives practical help real value.
Draft headline: “Luther says good works do not matter”
The exhibition draft claims that Luther thinks good works do not matter. His own statement praises practical help for people in need. Check whether the headline fairly represents what he says.
Blank proof paper
Blank paper for checking the passage before printing it for the exhibit.
The four-panel exhibit
The four completed panels compare the roadside story, the family feast, the feeding accounts and Luther's statement about practical help.
This passage contradicts the sweeping headline
Luther calls helping people in need a better deed. That contradicts the draft's blanket claim that good works do not matter, without settling all his views on faith and salvation.
A fairer headline: Luther commends practical help
Luther commends practical help for people in need. His statement and the roadside story both value care, but that similarity alone does not show that this passage caused his view.
Proof: our Luke 10:33–35 paraphrase
Our Luke 10:33–35 paraphrase in print

An optional fictional Mars journey: rescue the crew, investigate an ice core and bring an extraordinary specimen home. This imagined creature is not a report of real Martian life.
